analysis.investment_thesis: Mastek is a decent mid-tier IT services business trading at a modest 12.8x P/E with strong historical CAGR (23% revenue, 32% net profit over 9 years) and excellent FCF conversion — but the narrow moat, decelerating growth, and margin profile below top-tier IT peers limits its compounding potential. At this price, it is fair but not compelling enough to deploy significant capital.
key_strengths: Excellent FCF quality — FCF of INR 515 Cr exceeded net profit of INR 404 Cr in FY26, confirming high earnings quality (FCF/NI >100%)
ROCE of 18% above threshold with low leverage (D/E 0.20) and all 5 years OCF-positive — balance sheet discipline is commendable
Undemanding valuation at 12.8x P/E and 9.8x EV/EBITDA for a business that compounded net profit at 32.5% CAGR over 9 years
key_risks: Mid-tier IT services has weak moat — no pricing power, high people-dependency, and constant pressure from larger peers (TCS, Infosys, Wipro) and offshore challengers
Revenue growth visibly decelerating (3,055→3,455→3,699 Cr) while margins remain below category leaders (~14% vs 21%+ for top-tier IT)
Finance costs ballooned from INR 6 Cr (FY19) to INR 44 Cr (FY24), signaling acquisition-driven debt; EBITDA dipped in FY25 (535→455 Cr) despite revenue growth — margin discipline is not yet proven
red_flags: EBITDA compression in FY25 (535→455 Cr) even as revenue grew — absorbed costs from acquisitions without operating leverage, a hallmark of weak moat businesses
Promoter stake at only 35.77% is modest; combined with rising borrowings (INR 273 Cr in FY21 to INR 583 Cr in FY25), acquisition strategy warrants monitoring for capital allocation discipline
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Mastek has delivered impressive headline numbers — 23% revenue CAGR and 32.5% net profit CAGR over nine years — but inversion demands we ask: how durable is this? IT services at the mid-tier level is a commodity business. Clients can switch vendors, pricing is squeezed in renegotiations, and attrition is chronic. Operating margins of 14.1% compare unfavorably to TCS (~24%) or Infosys (~21%), revealing the absence of the pricing power that separates great businesses from merely adequate ones. The FY25 EBITDA dip to INR 455 Cr (from INR 535 Cr in FY24) — even as revenue grew from INR 3,055 Cr to INR 3,455 Cr — is the clearest symptom: when revenue grows but profits shrink, operating leverage is absent.

The positives are real and should not be dismissed: FCF exceeds reported net profit (INR 515 Cr vs. INR 404 Cr in FY26), which is a hallmark of honest accounting and asset-light economics. Debt-to-equity at 0.20 is conservative. And at 12.8x trailing earnings with a forward P/E of 11.3x, Mr. Market is not demanding payment for hope. But Munger's dictum — a great business at a fair price beats a fair business at a great price — cuts both ways: this is a fair business at a fair price, which produces fair returns. Without a discernible moat, Mastek is a HOLD for those already invested, but not a high-conviction addition.
